context: Nezi's drawer of loose plain socks in four colours: orange, pink, white and black. The total is stated, the orange, pink and white counts are stated, and the remaining socks are black. One sock is taken out at random.

params.why: the answer must need simplifying, because the stem asks for simplest form

stem: Nezi has {=T} loose socks in a drawer. {=o} of them are plain orange, {=p} are plain pink and {=w} are plain white. The remaining socks are plain black. A sock is taken out at random. Calculate the probability that it is pink or black. Give your answer as a fraction in simplest form.
solution: The black socks are the ones that remain: ${=T}-{=o}-{=p}-{=w}= {=k}$ black socks.
A sock cannot be both pink and black, so the events are mutually exclusive and $P(\text{pink or black})=P(\text{pink})+P(\text{black})$.
notes: Advanced twist taken from book 17e (the remaining socks are a group the stem never counts): the student first finds the black count by subtraction from the stated total, then adds two single-colour probabilities, then simplifies. The counts o, p, w are drawn at most T//3-1 each, so k = T-o-p-w is always at least 3. The require gcd(s, T) > 1 (equivalent to gcd(o+w, T) > 1) forces a genuine simplification step, so 'simplest form' in the stem is meaningful; every T offered is even, so the require is met in a large share of draws. The key is a plain fraction n/d in lowest terms. An alternative route (1 minus P(orange or white)) gives the same value, so blind solvers cannot legitimately disagree. No mcq is used, so no misconception ids are attached.
